title: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids
blurb: Identify the four macromolecules by monomer, bond, elements and function, and explain how enzymes work and what slows them down.
question: A patient who cannot digest milk sugar is told she lacks the enzyme lactase. What kind of molecule is lactose, what is it made of, how does lactase break it, and why would lactase stop working if it were boiled?

teach.h: Four big molecules, built from small ones
teach.body: Formal definition: macromolecules are large carbon-based (organic) molecules; most are polymers built from repeating monomers. Dehydration synthesis (condensation) joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis breaks polymers apart by adding water. Plain English: life builds its big molecules like beads on a string. Snapping a bead on squeezes out a water molecule; adding water snaps it back off. The four families are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

head: Macromolecule
Monomer
Bond
Main job
rows: Lipids (C, H, O; P in phospholipids)
Proteins (C, H, O, N, often S)
Nucleic acids (C, H, O, N, P)
teach.caption: Lipids are not true polymers. ATP is a modified nucleotide.

head: Carbohydrate
Made of / role
rows: Animal storage in liver and muscle
Plant cell walls; fiber humans cannot digest

teach.caption: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Phospholipid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate (hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tails). Steroids (cholesterol, sex hormones, cortisol) have four fused rings. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

teach.body: An amino acid has a central carbon with an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group; peptide bonds link them, and 9 are essential (must come from the diet in adults). Enzymes are mostly proteins and act as biological catalysts: they speed reactions by LOWERING activation energy, are not consumed, and do not change the energy released or the equilibrium. The substrate fits the active site (lock-and-key; induced fit). Names usually end in -ase: lactase breaks lactose.

teach.caption: Activity rises to an optimum, then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures. Each enzyme also has an optimum pH: pepsin approx. 2 (stomach), salivary amylase approx. 7, trypsin approx. 8 (small intestine).

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Best at its own optimum pH
Binds active site; beaten by more substrate
Metal ions (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺) or vitamin-derived helpers

teach.h: Worked scenario: Sofia and the missing lactase
teach.body: Sofia, a patient at a clinic where nursing applicant Ray volunteers, is lactose intolerant. Lactose is a disaccharide carbohydrate made of glucose + galactose. Lactase breaks it by hydrolysis, adding water to split the glycosidic bond. Without enough lactase, lactose passes undigested. Lactase tablets supply the missing enzyme, and because enzymes are reused, a small dose can digest a lot of lactose. Boiling them would ruin them: high heat denatures the protein, unfolding its active site so lactose no longer fits.

teach.text: Classic swaps: glycogen is ANIMAL storage, starch is PLANT storage; carbohydrates give the QUICKEST energy, lipids STORE the most; saturated fats have NO double bonds and are solid; hydrolysis BREAKS, dehydration synthesis BUILDS; enzymes LOWER activation energy, are not used up, and stop working when too hot; denaturation unfolds a protein but leaves its peptide bonds intact; sucrose is glucose + FRUCTOSE.

items: Dehydration synthesis builds (releases water); hydrolysis breaks (adds water).
Carbs: monosaccharides, glycosidic bonds, quick energy; starch (plant), glycogen (animal), cellulose (fiber).
Lipids: glycerol + fatty acids, ester bonds, 9 kcal/g; phospholipids build membranes.
Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds, nitrogen. Nucleic acids: nucleotides, phosphorus.
Enzymes lower activation energy, are reused, and depend on temperature, pH and substrate level.

summary: You can now identify carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids by their monomers, bonds, elements and functions, and explain dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis. You can also explain how enzymes lower activation energy and predict how temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors change their activity.

A.q: Which polysaccharide is the main energy-storage carbohydrate in animals, stored in the liver and muscle?
A.why: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, kept mainly in the liver and skeletal muscle.

whyNot.0: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants.
whyNot.2: Cellulose builds plant cell walls and is fiber humans cannot digest.
whyNot.3: Chitin is structural, found in fungal cell walls and insect exoskeletons.

A.q: Which element is found in all proteins but NOT in carbohydrates or triglycerides?
A.why: Every amino acid has an amino group containing nitrogen; carbohydrates and triglycerides contain only C, H and O.

whyNot.0: Oxygen is present in carbohydrates and triglycerides as well as proteins.
whyNot.1: Carbon is the backbone of all organic molecules, including carbohydrates and fats.
whyNot.2: Hydrogen is present in all four macromolecule groups.

A.q: What happens to an enzyme once the reaction it catalyzes is complete?
options: It is released unchanged for reuse
It is consumed and must be replaced
It becomes part of the final product
It is denatured by the energy released
A.why: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not consumed or changed by the reaction and can be used again.

whyNot.1: Catalysts are not used up; one enzyme molecule can act on many substrate molecules.
whyNot.2: The enzyme separates from the products after the reaction.
whyNot.3: Enzymes denature from high heat or extreme pH, not from catalyzing their normal reaction.

B.q: Sucrose (table sugar) is a disaccharide made of which two monosaccharides?
B.why: Sucrose = glucose + fructose, joined by a glycosidic bond.

whyNot.0: Glucose + galactose is lactose, the sugar in milk.
whyNot.3: Sucrose contains glucose; fructose + galactose is not one of the common disaccharides.

B.q: Butter is solid at room temperature while olive oil is liquid. Which explanation is correct?
options: Butter's fatty acids have no C=C double bonds
Butter's fatty acids have many C=C double bonds
Olive oil contains more glycerol per molecule
Olive oil is made of phospholipids, not fats
B.why: Butter is rich in saturated fatty acids (no C=C double bonds); their straight chains pack tightly, so it is solid.

whyNot.1: Double bonds create kinks that keep fats liquid; that describes the unsaturated fatty acids in olive oil.
whyNot.2: Every triglyceride has one glycerol, so glycerol content does not explain the difference.
whyNot.3: Olive oil is made of triglycerides (fats), mostly unsaturated, not phospholipids.

B.q: A human enzyme's activity is measured from 20 °C to 60 °C. Which result is expected?
options: Activity keeps rising steadily up to 60 °C
Activity is the same at every temperature
Activity is lowest near body temperature
B.why: Activity rises to an optimum near body temperature (approx. 37 °C) and then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures.

whyNot.0: Above the optimum, heat denatures the enzyme and activity drops.
whyNot.2: Temperature changes how fast molecules collide and whether the enzyme keeps its shape.
whyNot.3: Human enzymes work best near body temperature, not worst.

C.q: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach. If pepsin is placed in a solution at pH 8, what happens to its activity?
options: Activity rises; its optimum is near pH 8
Activity is unchanged; pH has no effect
Activity drops; its optimum is near pH 2
It becomes trypsin and digests protein
C.why: Pepsin's optimum is approx. pH 2 (stomach acid); at pH 8 it is far from its optimum, so activity drops.

whyNot.0: pH 8 is the optimum for trypsin in the small intestine, not pepsin.
whyNot.1: pH affects enzyme shape, so each enzyme works best at its own optimum.
whyNot.3: Changing pH does not turn one enzyme into another.

C.q: A protein is heated until it denatures. Which statement about it is correct?
options: Its peptide bonds break into free amino acids
It gains activity because more sites are exposed
It is turned into fatty acids and glycerol
It unfolds, but its amino acid sequence stays
C.why: Denaturation disrupts folding (shape), so function is lost, but the peptide bonds of the primary sequence remain intact.

whyNot.0: Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis; denaturation leaves them intact.
whyNot.1: Losing shape destroys the active site, so activity is lost, not gained.
whyNot.2: Fatty acids and glycerol come from lipids; heating does not convert proteins into them.

C.q: A drug binds the active site of an enzyme and blocks the substrate. Adding much more substrate restores the reaction rate. The drug is best described as a:
C.why: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site, so flooding the enzyme with substrate can outcompete it.

whyNot.1: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape, so extra substrate does not overcome it.
whyNot.2: Coenzymes help enzymes work; they do not block the active site.
whyNot.3: Metal ion cofactors such as Zn²⁺ or Mg²⁺ assist enzymes rather than inhibit them.

reteach.title: A grocery store for molecules
reteach.question: Picture four aisles in a grocery store: bread, butter, meat and the recipe-book section. How does each aisle match a macromolecule?

blocks.body: The bread and fruit aisle is carbohydrates: fast energy, built from simple sugars. The butter and oil aisle is lipids: dense, long-lasting energy (more than twice the calories per gram) and the stuff of cell membranes. The meat, eggs and beans aisle is proteins: built from amino acids, the body's tools and building blocks. The recipe books are nucleic acids: they store the instructions for making all the proteins. Enzymes are the store staff: they speed everything up and are never sold.

blocks.text: Butter stores the most energy, but bread gives it fastest: lipids store, carbohydrates fuel.

explain.body: Dehydration synthesis joins monomers and releases a water molecule. Hydrolysis adds water to split a polymer into monomers; digestion is hydrolysis.

test.q: Which process joins two glucose molecules into maltose?
options: Hydrolysis, which releases a water molecule
test.why: Joining monomers is dehydration synthesis, and a water molecule is released.

whyNot.0: Hydrolysis breaks polymers apart and uses water rather than releasing it.
whyNot.2: Hydrolysis with water would split maltose into glucose, the reverse of this reaction.
whyNot.3: Dehydration synthesis releases water; it does not add it.

explain.body: Carbohydrates: C, H, O; monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds; quick energy. Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids), phospholipids (2 fatty acids + phosphate), steroids (four rings); long-term storage and membranes.

test.q: A phospholipid differs from a triglyceride because a phospholipid has:
options: 3 fatty acids and a phosphate group
4 fused carbon rings instead of chains
2 fatty acids and a phosphate group
A glucose head instead of glycerol
test.why: A phospholipid is glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a phosphate group, giving a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.

whyNot.0: Three fatty acids is the triglyceride count.
whyNot.1: Four fused rings describes steroids such as cholesterol.
whyNot.3: Phospholipids are built on glycerol, not glucose.

explain.body: Proteins: 20 amino acids linked by peptide bonds; contain nitrogen; jobs include enzymes, hemoglobin, collagen, keratin, antibodies, insulin. Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA): nucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds; contain nitrogen and phosphorus.

test.q: Which monomers are joined by peptide bonds to form proteins?
test.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

whyNot.0: Nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids, joined by phosphodiester bonds.
whyNot.1: Monosaccharides build carbohydrates through glycosidic bonds.
whyNot.2: Fatty acids join glycerol by ester bonds to form lipids.

explain.body: Enzymes lower activation energy so reactions run faster at body temperature. The substrate binds the active site (lock-and-key, induced fit). Enzymes are reused, and they do not change the energy released or the equilibrium.

test.q: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in the body by:
test.why: Enzymes lower the activation energy needed to start a reaction, so it proceeds faster.

whyNot.1: Raising activation energy would slow the reaction down.
whyNot.2: Enzymes do not change the total energy released by the reaction.
whyNot.3: Enzymes speed up reaching equilibrium but do not change where it lies.
